absent: Wire encoding of capability query, time read, cross read and alarm messages exchanged with the device.
Conditions under which RTC-class or PTP initialization reports exposed versus silent skip beyond success signaling.
Layout and capacity constant of alarm buffers and queue feeding contract.
Behavior of request queue and alarm queue completion callbacks and wakeup path.
Power management ordering beyond freeze preserving wake and restore rebuilding queues.
Hardware timestamp parameter derivation and counter domain definitions.
Backend operation contracts for queue state, addresses, readiness, generation and affinity.
Ring creation, mapping, sizing and notification transport details.
Error values for device reset, queue deletion and device-ready transitions.
Concurrency beyond per-queue locking for alarm path versus clock paths.

findings.text: The PTP teardown helper has external linkage within the dossier and releases the associated PTP handle, freeing its wrapper with device-managed release only after a successful unregister.

Per-clock bring-up first queries capability details for the given selector and propagates query failure. RTC-class exposure is attempted only when its build option is active and the reported type belongs to the UTC family, while PTP exposure is attempted only when its build option is active. Negative outcomes from either exposure propagate, positive outcomes mark the clock visible, and a clock visible through neither path triggers a warning identifying selector, type and variant while still reporting overall success.

Clock collection start requires the device to report at least one clock and records that count, allocates tracking for later teardown, then brings up each selector in order. Any bring-up failure unwinds through the common teardown. Teardown clears each occupied tracking slot after attempting unregister with a warning on failure, then stops the RTC-class aggregate when present.

The internal header supplies disabled-build behavior where PTP unregister reports absence and class stop does nothing, contrasting with the active PTP object where unregister delegates to the PTP core and frees the wrapper on success.

Alarm queue feeding and kick preparation are guarded by the per-queue spin lock when the caller requests guarded operation. Initial queue setup initializes those locks before any use, the normal probe path uses guarded feeding plus guarded kick preparation, and the resume path uses unguarded feeding plus unguarded kick preparation.

Alarm buffer allocation uses device-managed zeroed storage for both the pointer list and each buffer of the requested capacity, records the list and element count on the device state, and reports allocation exhaustion without partial success.

Queue discovery selects one or two queues depending on alarm support, then initializes the corresponding per-queue locks. When alarms are present the alarm ring size is queried, an empty ring is rejected, buffers are allocated on first use or the retained count is clamped to the current ring size.

Probe links freshly allocated device state to the virtio device, discovers queues, marks the device ready, starts clocks, then arms alarms and notifies with unwind to clock teardown or full reset plus queue deletion on failure. Common removal stops clocks, resets the device and deletes queues. Freeze leaves the device unreset to preserve wake capability, while restore deletes queues, rediscovers them, re-arms alarms, marks ready and notifies, tearing down fully on failure.

The RTC driver object binds the clock device with wildcard matching, advertises the alarm feature only when RTC-class support is built in, and wires probe, removal, freeze and restore with sleep-aware helpers for the power transitions.

The match table pairs device type VIRTIO_ID_CLOCK with wildcard VIRTIO_DEV_ANY_ID followed by a zero terminator, and the feature table holds VIRTIO_RTC_F_ALARM when RTC-class support is enabled and is otherwise empty.

The PTP clock wrapper associates a PTP handle with its parent RTC device, embeds PTP operation descriptors, carries the numeric virtio clock selector, and records whether cross-timestamping is available.
The cross-timestamp context pairs a device time value with a system counter measurement for later combination.

A tiny getter copies the stored device time and counter measurement into caller outputs with unconditional success. A helper records the counter domain, reads paired device nanoseconds and cycles, rejects values beyond the maximum representable time, and converts the remainder to kernel time. The top handler requires cross capability, derives hardware parameters, requires the snapshot domain to match, performs the slow device read before invoking the generic combiner, and emits a debug message if combination fails.
Fine frequency adjustment, time offset adjustment, absolute time setting and generic enable all unconditionally report operation not supported.

Precise time read brackets the device read with system timestamp capture on both sides, rejects device values exceeding the signed maximum as invalid, and otherwise converts nanoseconds to calendar form.

The PTP operation template assigns module ownership and binds handlers for fine adjustment, offset adjustment, precise read, absolute set, generic enable and cross-timestamping, leaving the descriptive name to be fixed per clock type.
The vDPA adaptation nests a generic virtio device alongside its backend handle and cached feature bits.
Module metadata declares version 0.1, author Jason Wang at jasowang@redhat.com, description vDPA bus driver for virtio devices, and license GPL v2.

Configuration access, status access, reset and queue notification all delegate to the backend operations. Generation uses an optional backend query and defaults to zero, both plain and data-bearing notifications report success after kicking, configuration interrupts forward a change indication and return handled, and queue interrupts forward the ring handler outcome.

Successful queue creation requires a non-null name, an index within backend range, an idle backend slot and a non-zero size. Feature VIRTIO_F_NOTIFICATION_DATA is retained only when the backend offers the corresponding kick. The created ring records its maximum size, preserves the address map for the first queue, programs negotiated size and descriptor plus driver plus device addresses, resets split or packed state, installs callbacks and marks ready.
Address programming or state programming failure deletes the freshly created ring, clears backend readiness on a best-effort basis, warns if readiness persists, and returns an error pointer.
Single queue deletion deactivates backend readiness on a best-effort basis before deleting the ring, and bulk deletion safely walks the device queue list applying that behavior to each entry.

Default affinity grouping uses a single set covering all affine vectors. Mask construction accounts for leading and trailing non-affine vectors, installs the default grouping when none is supplied, allocates one mask per vector, marks non-affine vectors universal, distributes affine vectors evenly across groups, and reports allocation failure without leaking.

Queue set creation optionally builds affinity masks, leaves unnamed entries null, creates named entries with dense backend indices, applies per-queue affinity when supported, registers the configuration-change callback, and releases masks. Any creation failure deletes all queues and releases masks before propagating the error.

Feature query delegates to the backend, finalization allows the ring layer to adjust features before committing them to the backend, the bus name derives from the backend device name, and per-queue affinity update delegates when supported and otherwise reports success.
An alarm ring reporting zero capacity is rejected as insufficient space, and previously allocated buffers are never used beyond the smaller of the retained count and the current ring size.
Both cross-timestamp and precise read paths validate device nanoseconds against kernel maxima and report invalid argument instead of wrapping or truncating.
The internal header defines a once-only inclusion guard macro.
